Female Deepwater sculpin reach a maximum total length of 23 centimeters [Li = 23 centimeters], a modest size compared to many other cottid species inhabiting North American freshwater systems. This asymptotic length, derived from field surveys of mature individuals across the species’ range in deep glacial lakes, is accompanied by a corresponding ultimate wet weight of 129.5 grams [Wwi = 129.5 grams] for adult females. The length-weight relationship follows a standard power function typical of benthic fishes, reflecting a robust, heavy-bodied morphology adapted for life in cold, dark profundal zones. These values were estimated from specimens collected in Lake Michigan and several smaller Canadian Shield lakes, where the species shows relatively consistent growth trajectories across populations. Adult sculpin are characterized by a broad head, large pectoral fins, and a tapering posterior, all features consistent with a sedentary, sit-and-wait predatory lifestyle on the lake bottom.

Reproductive output in Deepwater sculpin has been characterized primarily through laboratory observations conducted under stable thermal regimes. Females maintained at a constant water temperature of 7 °C [T = 7 °C] deposit approximately 481 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 481 eggs per spawning event] in a single annual event [F_R_i = single annual event]. This annual fecundity is moderate among cottids and reflects the species’ relatively slow life history, which is constrained by low ambient temperatures and limited food resources in oligotrophic hypolimnetic habitats. The estimate is based on gravid females measuring around 13 centimeters in total length, a size at which most individuals within a population have completed their first reproductive season. Egg diameters in this species typically range from 1.5 to 2.2 millimeters, yielding a wet weight at birth of approximately 0.0042 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0042 grams] for each newly hatched larva following eclosion. This small initial mass aligns with a lecithotrophic strategy in which the yolk-sac larva depends entirely on endogenous reserves during its first days after hatching.

The life span of Deepwater sculpin is remarkably extended for a fish of its body size, a trait widely shared among cold-water benthic species. Under natural thermal conditions characteristic of its deep-lake habitat, maintained year-round at approximately 7 °C [T = 7 °C], the maximum recorded longevity reaches 7 years [am = 7 years], and puberty is attained only after 3 years following hatching [tp = 3 years following hatching], both measured under this stable thermal environment. This extended lifespan is accompanied by a protracted juvenile phase; field studies and captive-rearing observations indicate that the delayed maturation represents a significant investment in somatic growth before the onset of reproductive activity, a pattern that is ecologically sensible given the low and predictable productivity of the profundal zone.

Comparative analyses with other members of the genus Myoxocephalus reveal that Deepwater sculpin exhibits one of the lowest fecundities relative to body size, a trait that has been linked to its specialization for deep, cold, and unproductive lake environments. The annual egg production of 481 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = 481 eggs per spawning event] in a single event annually [F_R_i = single event annually] is substantially lower than that of its marine congener, the shorthorn sculpin (Myoxocephalus scorpius), which may release several thousand eggs per spawning event in coastal waters. This discrepancy is partially attributable to the smaller body size of M. thompsonii, but also reflects the energetic constraints imposed by the chronically low temperatures (7 °C [T = 7 °C]) and limited prey availability of its habitat. The egg size, however, is comparable, with diameters between 1.5 and 2.2 millimeters producing larvae that are relatively large for a sculpin of this size at the point of hatching. The species thus appears to balance reproductive investment by producing fewer, larger offspring that are better provisioned to survive the challenges of an oligotrophic environment.

Physiological studies of Deepwater sculpin have focused on metabolic adaptations that allow it to thrive in the thermally stable profundal zone of large lakes. The consistently low year-round temperature of approximately 7 °C [T = 7 °C] defines the species’ metabolic scope and constrains growth rates, reproduction, and activity levels. At this temperature, routine metabolic rates are markedly depressed compared to those of epilimnetic fishes, representing an energy-saving strategy that underpins the species’ extended maximum lifespan of 7 years [am = 7 years] and its delayed sexual maturation at 3 years after hatching [tp = 3 years after hatching] at a temperature of 7 °C [T = 7 °C] at a temperature of 7 °C [T = 7 °C]. This slow pace of life is further reflected in the low egg production of approximately 481 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 481 eggs per spawning event] in a single annual event [F_R_i = single annual event], a rate that is sustained over several reproductive seasons due to the iteroparous breeding strategy of this cottid. Ultimately, the combination of small body length (23 centimeters [Li = 23 centimeters]), modest adult mass (129.5 grams [Wwi = 129.5 grams]), and small larval size (approximately 0.0042 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0042 grams]) illustrates a life history finely tuned to the stable but resource-poor conditions of the deep, cold lakes that this species calls home.
